newsitem.title: GERMANY: German FDP casts doubt on foreign worker clampdown.
newsitem.headline: German FDP casts doubt on foreign worker clampdown.

text.p: Germany's Free Democrats (FDP), junior partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government, expressed misgivings on Wednesday over conservative calls to impose stricter controls on foreigners working in Germany.

FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle said a law setting quotas on the number of foreigners allowed into Germany would be a better way to deal with the problem of immigration. His party would present such a bill next month, he said.

A number of parliamentary deputies for Kohl's Christian Democrats and many in their arch-conservative Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), believe it should be made more difficult for foreigners to get work permits as unemployment among Germans soars to record levels.

Some CSU members also favour limiting the number of Jewish immigrants allowed to enter Germany from the former Soviet Union under a special 1990 agreement. Westerwelle did not comment on this proposal but said the work permit plan was misguided.

"I have my doubts whether it's really clever to make social security payments the only income possibility for foreigners," Westerwelle said. "I'm happy when foreigners who live here take up work here and provide for their families themselves."

"What's much more important is the basic question of whether we in Germany need stronger immigration control, or even better an immigration control law. That's what we're suggesting," Westerwelle told North German Radio.
Under the FDP's plans, Germany would select immigrants according to its needs, giving preference to people who could do particular jobs or who were from a certain age group.

It would clamp down harder on non-European Union foreigners who currently come to Germany, mostly as asylum seekers and ethnic Germans from eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union, but try to ensure better integration of those who are accepted.
This would also mean making it easier for foreigners born in Germany to get German citizenship. The CDU is split on this issue while the CSU is fiercely opposed to the FDP stance.
Foreign children can currently become German only if they give up their claim to the citizenship of any other country.
Around seven million of Germany's 80 million population are foreigners, most of whom have lived here for many years.
Around a quarter were born in Germany, many the children of "guest workers" from Turkey, Yugoslavia and other countries who helped create Germany's postwar "economic miracle".

Officially, Germany does not accept immigration by foreigners from outside the EU. But every year it takes in tens of thousands of asylum seekers, and people of German descent from former Soviet republics and eastern Europe.
